title: Wages growth lifts to 3.4% on care-worker and public-sector pay rises, but productivity is flat
summary: Shows the wages, productivity and inflation link: pay rises ordered by the Fair Work Commission lifted wage growth while labour productivity has not increased in almost a decade.
lede: Annual wages growth rose to 3.4% in March 2025 from 3.2% in December, driven by Fair Work Commission pay rises for childcare and aged care workers and new state public-sector deals. Economists warned the rate is not sustainable without productivity growth, though they expected the RBA to keep cutting.

terms.def: Wages push up prices, which push wages up again.
Output produced per hour worked.
ABS measure of changes in the price of labour, holding job quality constant.

figures.label: Childcare workers' pay rise in the quarter

angle: Use it to show cost-push risk: wages growing faster than productivity raise unit labour costs, which could feed inflation and limit how far the RBA can cut.

questions.q: Explain why wages growth faster than productivity growth can lead to higher inflation.
Outline one role of the Fair Work Commission in wage determination.

note: Older item (published May 2025): figures are as at that date; check for newer data before quoting. Newspaper article reproduced for classroom use. Treasurer and economists' comments are opinion; check ABS release for the latest Wage Price Index.

title: Workers lose over $4.7 billion a year in unpaid super and the ATO rarely penalises employers
summary: Case of a gap between the legal safety net for workers and its enforcement, with the superannuation guarantee rising to 12% and payday super proposed as a fix.
lede: The ATO recovered only 17% of the $4.7 billion in unpaid super for 2020-21, and fewer than half of penalties went beyond repaying the missing amount. The superannuation guarantee rose from 11.5% to 12% on 1 July 2025 and payday super is proposed to cut non-payment.

terms.def: Compulsory employer contribution, a percentage of ordinary earnings, into a worker's super fund.
Proposal that super is paid on the same day as wages.
Minimum standards and entitlements protecting workers.

figures.label: Share of unpaid super recovered by the ATO
Workers not receiving full super entitlements
figures.source: Super Members Council via ABC News

figures.label: Penalties above remediation of the unpaid amount
Super paid after employee referrals / penalties

angle: Use as an example of a limitation of labour market policy: a minimum entitlement is only as effective as its enforcement.

questions.q: Outline one limitation of labour market policies, using unpaid super as an example.
Explain how payday super could improve the effectiveness of the superannuation guarantee.

note: Older item (published Jun 2025): figures are as at that date; check for newer data before quoting. Newspaper article reproduced for classroom use. The latest ATO figures quoted are for 2020-21.

title: Big companies quit the Climate Active carbon-neutral scheme over integrity concerns
summary: A real-world case on the limits of voluntary, market-based environmental schemes: doubts about offset quality are driving firms away from buying credits.
lede: More than 100 companies, including Australia Post, Telstra and Canva, have left the voluntary Climate Active scheme in two years amid greenwashing and offset-integrity concerns. The federal government is considering reshaping or shutting the scheme.

terms.def: A credit for emissions avoided or removed elsewhere, bought to cancel out emissions.
Australian Carbon Credit Unit; one tonne of abatement.
Misleading claims about environmental benefits.

figures.label: Companies that have left Climate Active in two years
Share of offsets bought from global projects
Price of some international nature-based credits

angle: Use when evaluating market-based instruments: they depend on trust and measurement, and weak integrity can undermine the price signal.

questions.q: Outline one disadvantage of using carbon offsets to meet emissions targets.
Explain why the integrity of carbon credits matters for market-based environmental policy.

note: Older item (published Feb 2025): figures are as at that date; check for newer data before quoting. Newspaper article reproduced for classroom use. Climate Active is a voluntary offset register, not the Safeguard Mechanism.

title: China's shadow stalls Taiwan's bid to join the CPTPP
summary: Illustrates how geopolitics shapes regional trade agreements and why consensus rules slow enlargement of a trading bloc.
lede: Taiwan's representative in Canberra urged Australia, as incoming chair of the CPTPP, to put Taiwan's application on the agenda, saying it should be judged on economic merit. Members have avoided considering China's and Taiwan's bids, while Costa Rica leapfrogged both.

terms.def: Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, a regional trade agreement.
A group of countries that give each other preferential trade terms.
The process of a new member joining an agreement.

figures.label: Taiwan's rank as a destination for Australian exports

angle: Good for the advantages and disadvantages of multilateral and regional agreements: gains from market access versus political constraints on expansion.

questions.q: Outline one advantage of regional trade agreements such as the CPTPP for Australia.
Explain why membership decisions in a trading bloc can be slowed by non-economic factors.

title: China's Belt and Road investment and construction hits a record in the first half of 2025
summary: Evidence on shifting foreign investment flows and China's growing economic influence in developing economies as US tariffs rise.
lede: Chinese construction contracts and investment in Belt and Road countries reached $124bn in the first half of 2025, more than all of 2024, according to a Griffith University study. Researchers link the surge to slow domestic growth, supply-chain diversification and the US tariff trade war.

terms.def: Investment that gives the investor lasting control or a significant interest in a business abroad.
China's global infrastructure and investment programme launched in 2013.
Criticism that heavy lending leaves borrowers dependent on the lender.

title: Deloitte: strong jobs and wages, but productivity must follow
summary: A compact data set on April 2025 labour market strength, wage growth by sector and falling labour productivity.
lede: Deloitte Access Economics notes 89,000 jobs were added in April with unemployment steady at 4.1% and participation at a near-record 67.1%. Wage growth returned to 3.4% annually but labour productivity is 5.7% below its March 2022 peak.

terms.def: Labour force as a share of the working-age population.
Employed workers who want and are available for more hours.
Industries such as health, education and public administration where output is not sold at market prices.

angle: Use for labour market analysis: low unemployment and high participation, with wage growth only sustainable if productivity improves.

questions.q: Calculate what is meant by the participation rate and state its value in April 2025.
Explain why productivity growth is needed for sustainable wage growth.

note: Older item (published May 2025): figures are as at that date; check for newer data before quoting. Secondary source: Deloitte Access Economics email newsletter reproduced for classroom use; ABS data should be checked at source.

title: Trump flags a new baseline tariff of 15 to 20 per cent on the rest of the world
summary: A current protectionism case: higher US baseline tariffs and bilateral deals, and what they mean for Australian exporters.
lede: President Trump said the US would set a baseline tariff of 15 to 20% for most countries, above the 10% Australia currently faces. Australian meat, gold and pharmaceutical exporters, almost half of US-bound exports, would be exposed, while the UK has locked in a 10% rate.

terms.def: A tax on imported goods.
A minimum tariff rate applied to most trading partners.
A trade deal between two countries.

figures.label: Australian goods sold to the US subject to the lowest rate
UK baseline tariff locked in; steel and aluminium

angle: Use to show how a major trading partner's protectionism affects Australia's exports, and why bilateral deals can lock in lower rates.

questions.q: Outline two effects of a tariff on an importing country.
Explain how higher US tariffs could affect Australian exporters.

title: ANU research: tax and transfer system leaves older Australians better off than the young
summary: Evidence for intergenerational inequality in the tax-transfer system, with a call to broaden the tax base and tackle bracket creep.
lede: ANU researchers find the average 75-year-old's post-tax income now equals the national average, up from about 75% 25 years ago, and is one-third higher than for 18 to 30 year olds. They say about one-third of income escapes tax and argue reform should broaden the tax base.

terms.def: Wage growth pushes taxpayers into higher tax brackets so tax rises as a share of income.
The income, wealth or spending that is taxed.
Fairness in the sharing of costs and benefits between generations.

angle: Use for the distribution of income and wealth and the effect of the budget on redistribution: it challenges the assumption that transfers always go to the least well off.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by bracket creep.
Assess the extent to which the tax and transfer system redistributes income fairly across age groups.

title: Modelling for the Productivity Commission: GST causes least economic harm per dollar raised
summary: Gives numbers on the efficiency of different taxes, useful for evaluating tax reform and the features of a good tax.
lede: Modelling by Chris Murphy for the Productivity Commission finds that, per dollar raised, GST does the least economic harm, then personal income tax, then company tax. A package cutting the company tax rate and adding a cash flow tax could lift GDP by 0.5% over a decade.

terms.def: The economic harm from a tax's disincentive effects per extra dollar of revenue raised.
A tax on a company's cash inflows less outflows.
How little a tax distorts decisions to work, save and invest.

title: FIRB delays put an $800m Chinese purchase of solar farms on the brink of collapse
summary: A case on regulating foreign investment: national-interest screening can slow the capital needed for renewable energy targets.
lede: The $813m sale of five solar farms by Lightsource bp to Chinese government-backed Beijing Energy was held up for almost 14 months by the Foreign Investment Review Board. The delay highlights a trade-off between national security screening and meeting the 82% renewables target.
